speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I beg leave under standing order 31 to move the adjournment of the house for the purpose of discussing a definite matter of urgent public importance and the necessity of immediate action being taken iby this house to investigate the present financial position of the Sun Life Assurance Company of Canada and the conduct of its senior officials, as disclosed Iby the recent police court investigation in Chicago into the affairs of Samuel Insull and Martin Insull, now indicted by the United States government on charges of embezzlement and larceny.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT TO DISCUSS MATTER OF PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext:
I would direct the attention of the hon. member particularly to subsection 2 of the rule which regulates the procedure in regard to an application such as he is now making. Subsection 2 of standing order 31 reads:
The member desiring to make such a motion rises in his place, asks leave to move the adjournment of the house for the purpose of discussing a definite matter of urgent public importance, and states the matter.
Stating the matter does not go so far as to include discussing the matter. A statement of the matter is a description, an identification of the matter to be discussed, and I must ask the hon. member to state the matter. If he has stated the matter; if the subject to be discussed is an investigation of the affairs of the Sun Life Assurance Company, then he must proceed according to the terms of the rest of the standing order. To enter into any lengthy discussion of the matter would be an evasion of the rule, and out of order.

speechtext:
The hon. member for
West Elgin courteously notified me of his intention to make this application; I have had an opportunity of considering it and will not need to delay the house further by examining the statement. Under standing order No. 31 leave may be obtained to present a motion for the adjournment of the house for the purpose of discussing a definite matter of urgent public importance. The procedure is as follow's:	At the proper time the member rises in his place, asks leave to move the adjournment of the house for the purpose of discussing a definite matter of urgent public importance, and states the matter. He then hands a written statement of the matter proposed to be discussed to the Speaker who, if he thinks it in order and of urgent public importance, reads it out and asks whether the member has leave of the house to move the adjournment for the purpose stated. A motion under this standing order must be restricted to a single specific matter of recent occurrence. The authority for that statement will be found in the thirteenth edition of May at page 247.
In my opinion this is not a matter of recent occurrence, nor is the matter urgent. There must be a prima facie case of urgency. I refer again to May, thirteenth edition, page 247. The matter is not so urgent that the proceedings of the house should be halted so that it may be discussed now. The rules provide other opportunities for discussing such a matter.
For these reasons I hold that the application is not in order and should not be granted.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE MOTION FOR APPROVAL OF TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM

speechtext: The house resumed from Monday, October 31, consideration of the motion of Right Hon. R. B. Bennett (Prime Minister) for approval of the trade agreement entered into at Ottawa the 20th day of August, 1932, between representatives of His Majesty's government in Canada and His Majesty's government in the United Kingdom, subject to the legislation required in order to give effect to the fiscal changes consequent thereon.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE MOTION FOR APPROVAL OF TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I must
admit, at the outset, that what few arguments I intend to offer in this debate will have no convincing effect on my good friends on the other side of the house. At any rate, such is not my ambition. However, having been sent here by a partly agricultural and partly industrial constituency, a section of which is represented in the Quebec Legislative Assembly by the honourable the prime minister of my province, I feel bound to set forth my views on the agreements concluded last summer in Ottawa and-with due deference to my colleague, Mr. Taschereau-I may add that my good constituents are of the same opinion.
Before rising in this house to speak on this question, I thought it well to read over the history of trade relations between Canada and Great Britain, or rather, between Great Britain and what was formerly called its colonies, in order to familiarize myself with the evolution that has taken place in that sphere, evolution that developed itself along with the assertion of the rights of the dominions as members of the British Commonwealth of nations.
Glancing forty or fifty years back, considering the trend of events in the meantime, and then examining the conclusions arrived at by the representatives of Great Britain and of the dominions, which summarize the advantages and concessions extended by Canada to Great Britain as well as to other dominions, I deem

United Kingdom
it my duty, as a Canadian, to support these agreements not only because they are beneficial to Canada, advantageous for the contracting parties, but also because they are in themselves a demonstration to the civilized world of what may be done by well-intentioned and conscientious men towards alleviating the world depression.
If a happy solution has been found, which does not, I admit absolutely end our troubles, but surely alleviates them, we owe it, according to the testimony of those who took part in the conference-to which I shall refer again in a moment-we owe it to the man who day in and day out devotes his energy, his health, his splendid courage to promote the welfare of those whom it is his desire to see happier and more prosperous: the right honourable Prime Minister.of Canada (Mr. Bennett).
The other day I heard, and read in the Hansard, the address delivered by my hon. friend the former Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe). His chief argument-and I would be greatly surprised to see him use the same argument in his own constituency-was that he feared that the direct result of the agreements would be to cause friction, discontent and misunderstandings likely to affect adversely the now existing relations between Canada and Great Britain, and even to endanger the unity of the empire. As I was listening to his remarks, it seemed to me that I was dreaming. And still, I remember how, in the days of my youth, I used to go and hear, in the district I now represent, the speeches of the former member for Kamouraska. He was then the fiery opponent of closer relations, between Great Britain and the dominions. How times are changed! How can he be now such a staunch supporter of a non-development policy in connection with our relations, both economic and political, with Great Britain, in days gone by, from 1911 to 1921, he would never miss an opportunity to proclaim his faith in nationalism? Would it be that he seeks forgiveness for the errors of his youth? He may also have perceived that it was the best way of enlisting for himself the good will of the imperialist section of his party in anticipation of the day- nearer at hand than we may think-when it might please the Liberal group to substitute the former Minister of Justice to the present leader of the party. Then we would witness again the double dealing which seems to be the first plank in the liberal platform and which has proved so long a boon to the party in the province of Quebec as well as in the other provinces of the dominion: fierce nationalism in the province of Quebec and narrow imperialism in the other provinces. The
hon. member for Quebec has no cause for apprehension. History shows that, as the world changes and as statesmen are being faced with ever recurring and frequently unforeseen problems, the British Empire goes on and becomes, for the nations it is made of, a splendid testing and experimenting ground1, on account of its practical, constructive spirit, and chiefly on account of those tentative policies, which are, so to speak, inherent to the genius of these peoples.
No, there is no cause for alarm. Great Britain, of all the present day nations, gave to the world the example of freedom; old England is always solid and the survival of the British Empire is not bound with the existence of trade agreements. The resources of the empire are boundless and its greatest asset is perhaps that national spirit, which in the past, has cleared the atmosphere laden with apprehensions, uncertainties and oftentimes with danger; it is that loyalty to the crown still considered by the nations of the commonwealth as the symbol of their strength and unity.
With his vast experience, the former Minister of Justice is fully aware of the fact, The form, as well as the existence, of the British commonwealth does not lie in written laws, it does not lie in logic, in agreements or treaties, but resides in the continuous growth of a spirit and method particular to herself because they are in agreement with her tastes.
The agreements signed at Ottawa do not affect in any way the personal union existing between Great Britain and the dominions. To use the words of a French newspaperman, the sovereign is the only constitutional link between the various parts of the empire and the living symbol of imperial unity. Such a condition is wondered at by the other nations in the world, but for us it is quite natural.
For half a century, statesmen, both in the United Kingdom and in the dominions, have been constantly in search of a practical solution for the problems arising from trade relations between the nations of the British commonwealth.
Chamberlain, who was Secretary for the Colonies in the days of Lord Salisbury was surely of the British statesmen who concentrated their efforts in that direction, the one who did the most in that respect.
But should Chamberlain return to life now, notwithstanding what some hon. friends opposite may say, these agreements would certainly cause him to wonder at their contents and be far from satisfactory to him.
752	COMMONS
Imperial Conference-Trade Agreements
It was at the conference of 1894, held in Ottawa, between the different representatives of the British colonies and which was attended, not officially but unofficially, by a representative from Great Britain, that for the first time since the adoption of the policy advocated by the Manchester school of thought, was raised the question of asking Great Britain to abandon its free trade policy.
In 1895, when Chamberlain became Secretary for the Colonies, three main proposals concerning our trade relations were discussed.
Out of the three proposals two were discarded by Chamberlain as quite unacceptable. In a few moments we shall see how the spirit of the resolutions submitted by the colonial representatives in 1894 and which -were unequivocally rejected by Great Britain-and later by Chamberlain-is to be found again in the agreements signed here last summer. The very principle of these resolutions is contained in the treaties of 1932.
The analysis of these proposals leads us to recognize that the development of our trade relations has taken place along the same lines as our political and constitutional evolution.
The following was the only proposal agreed to by Chamberlain:
Free trade would be applied to practically the whole of the empire, hut the different contracting parties would be free to make their own arrangements as to the foreign products competing with certain commodities produced in abundance by the colonies, such as wheat, meat, wool, sugar and a few others yet that are consumed in large quantities by the mother country, and could, as a result of such an agreement, be totally produced in the colonies and by British labour.
Do not such proposals differ totally from the agreements signed here last summer?
Another proposal discussed in the days of Chamberlain was that of compelling the colonies to abandon their tariff policy and adopt a tariff for revenue. The colonies flatly rejected the proposal; such a policy could not be accepted by them. Owing to the existence of a protectionist feeling in the colonies, because of their infant industries, and specially owing to the fact that most of them were drawing their revenue from the customs duties, they rejected the offers.
The third proposal submitted by the colonial delegates at the conference held in Ottawa, in 1894, but declared unacceptable by the mother country who peremptorily refused to endorse it, was as follows-it is also in principle contained in the Ottawa agreements of 1932: The signing by Great Britain and the
[Mr. Dorion.1
colonies, of an agreement whereby the internal trade of the empire would be put on a more favourable basis than the trade intercourse between its various component parts and foreign countries. The colonies would still arrange their tariff as they would see fit, but they would agree to lower preferential duties in favour of British products. On the other hand, the mother country was to impose import duties on products similar to colonial products imported from other countries, while those from the colonies would be admitted free or granted a preference.
The last proposal of agreement meant that Great Britain would have had to abandon its free trade policy, and Chamberlain rejected it.
As I said a moment ago, those who claim that the agreements signed in Ottawa last summer mean a step backwards, are greatly mistaken, in my opinion. In no part of these agreements, treaties or understandings can be found the slightest indication of a commercial union such as was suggested by Chamberlain and the establishment of which was to be the first step towards an imperial federation.
Between 1894 and 1932, several conferences were held, and practically in every case, the question of trade relations was dealt with. In the meantime, a constitutional evolution was in process and led to the adoption of the following definition, in 1926:
Great Britain and the Dominions are autonomous communities within the British Empire, equal in status, in no way subordinate one to another in any aspect of their domestic or external affairs, though united by a common allegiance to the crown, and freely associated as members of the British commonwealth of nations.
It was in the spirit of that resolution that the Ottawa agreements were signed. They are actual treaties concluded between free countries, just as those signed by foreign countries between themselves. The concluding of these agreements does not affect, in any respect, the absolute freedom of either of the contracting parties.
Just a word, now, on the contents of the agreements. The Ottawa conference was instructed to find, after a thorough investigation, the best way to develop trade between the various parts of the empire. Are we justified, from the conclusions of the conference, to say that the end in view was reached? We believe so, although the results, on the whole, may not be felt within a month or two; that is obvious. The main objective, in connection with the conference, may I say again, was not, as was aimed at by Chamberlain, to make of the empire an economic entity, in other

United Kingdom
words a stepping stone to imperial federation, but rather to find the means of promoting trade within the empire.
While retaining their autonomy and freedom, the members of the empire, by means of real treaties, are granting certain advantages in their respective markets in connection with foreign goods, and it is unquestionable that the advantages obtained by Canada enable us to take away from the foreign competitors a substantial part of the British market. In return for the sacrifices consented to by the British consumer, a market will be secured here for some of the manufactured products of Great Britain. May I add that the chances of success of the conference were depending, above all, upon the spirit of sacrifice, the broadness of vision of our manufacturers, and regardless of what our friends of the Liberal party may say, the Canadian manufacturers have made real sacrifices in order to be of further assistance to the agricultural class in Canada.
Through these agreements, Great Britain made in our favour a two-fold concession: the free entry of certain goods and raw products; preferential rates on certain other goods. Up to 1930, that is until the return to power of the Conservative party, Great Britain enjoyed certain preferences in our markets but with no corresponding advantages accruing to us in the British market. Now, Great Britain will admit free of duty a certain number of our chief industrial and agricultural products, of which those of especial interest to the province of Quebec are: paper, aluminum, furs, textile products, asbestos, chemicals, creamery butter, cheese, eggs, salmon, codfish, apples, wheat, rye, copper, and so forth.
By these agreements, practically the whole range of our natural products will enjoy preferences varying from 10 to 33J per cent. In so far as my own province is specially concerned, these preferential rates shall apply to the following natural commodities: tobacco, prunes, honey, potatoes, etc. On the other hand, Canada gets certain advantages that will prove beneficial to the Canadian consumer. A certain class of commodities shall be admitted free of duty in this country while others will enjoy intermediary or general rates on similar products from other countries.
One of my hon. friends opposite expressed his surprise the other day-I think it was the hon. member for Bagot (Mr. Dumaine)-at the preference granted by the agreements on spirits. I am satisfied that as far as we, of the province of Quebec, are concerned that preference will be of no value. The Quebec Liquor Commission will be the only one to derive any benefit 53719-48	r
from it and Mr. Taschereau, whose government is particularly noted for the imposition of ever increasing taxes, shall certainly take advantage of the preference to raise the provincial taxes already levied by him on alcoholic beverages.
In spite of the opinion expressed by the hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Howard) I believe that the preferences to be enjoyed, in our market, on creamery equipment, shall not raise the price. On the contrary, that preference will be of a great help to our farmers in enabling them to buy such equipment at lower prices from British manufacturers.
Neither can we find in these agreements anything likely to lead to the conclusion that any of our present markets are being closed to us.
A few of our friends on the other side of the bouse are eagerly awaiting the results of the impending elections in the United States in the hope of renewing trade relations with the great republic to the south. The leaders of the two major political parties in the United States, in order to ease the anxiety of the farming community, have in fact just stated that no change would be made in the tariff now protecting American agriculture.
I have also heard several of our friends opposite speak of markets being lost to Canada as a direct result of the Ottawa agreements.
But, tell me, where are those markets? So far not a single one has been mentioned. And in what respect are these agreements an impediment to the conclusion of other treaties with other countries? The contrary is what happens. To the markets already available for our industries and for our farmers is being added a new one capable of absorbing from 75 to 100 million dollars worth of trade.
Some of our friends on the other side of the house are wondering at the fact that for some commodities the duration of the agreement is to be of five years and that, in respect to others, the limit is three years. What is their aim? What do they want? Have they an amendment to submit one way or the other? For some of them-the leader of the opposition, for instance-a period of five years is too long, while in the opinion of others-namely, the hon member for Bellechasse (Mr. Boulanger)-a term of three years is too short. I am not surprised to find such a difference of opinion among our friends. They advocate all kinds of policies, that being the creed of their party. They are imperialists when with imperialists; nationalists with nationalists; capitalists with capitalists-for instance, in the case of the Beauharnois affair-socialists with

754	COMMONS
Imperial Conference-Trade Agreements
socialists; free-traders with free-traders; protectionists with protectionists and radicals with the radicals. I say it again, in line with the principle of their party they undergo a complete change of mind overnight. The rotation of the earth around its axis from one day to the next is of longer duration than the political leanings of our friends.
As the right, hon. Prime Minister said when he laid the text of the agreements on the table of the house, these conventions are merely the forerunners of others of still greater benefit. Once again, I claim that these agreements, in the spirit of their author, were not supposed to bring about an immediate cessation of our troubles, but they surely will alleviate the hardships we are going through at the present time. No matter how hard man may work or how patiently he may seek for a solution of his problems, Providence alone rewards our effort and good will.
Any citizen concerned with public affairs is bound to cooperate to the best of his ability towards the solution of the problems arising from the hardships now enduring throughout the world.
These agreements have not been concluded without some difficulties. Nevertheless a great stride has been made and they represent a vast effort; it now remains for us to take advantage of them.
However I am sorry, Mr. Speaker, to note that the government in office in my own province seems to do nothing whatever in order to reap the benefit accruing from these agreements in which our farmers are so particularly concerned. While the governments of the other provinces have had, for a long time, their own representatives instructed to acquaint themselves on the spot with the requirements of the British markets, specially in connection with the quality of the products required and their presentation to the buyer, my own province, may I say again, has done nothing in that direction. What are they waiting for? Why should they be content with a fruitless opposition? I understand that the agreements may not please the prime minister of the province of Quebec because they do not favour exclusively the big interests of which he is the recognized champion, but it seems to me that he should have a little regard for the common people, the small wage earner, the primary producers, the farming class of his province. May the day come when we shall no longer see the shipment of Canadian products through American channels, and if, in order to reach that goal, freight rates, both by rail and by water, must be
tMr. Dorion.]
lowered, it would be in order to make the change.
At the beginning of my remarks, Mr. Speaker, I made the statement that the principle of understanding, of cooperation, between the various nations of the British commonwealth, which was the basis of the Ottawa economic conference, shall be held as an example to the other nations of the world at the coming world's economic conference. In association with the other parts of the empire, our country has given a splendid example to the civilized world. But, it must be admitted, the most urgent remedy, the most imperative at this hour of universal crisis with its resultant political and social disturbances in many other countries, is the restoration of confidence and hope in the minds of all. But, here in Canada, what use are they making of their time those whom the people have refused to entrust with the management of affairs? They are endeavouring to inspire mistrust, to weaken energies and courages, and to bereave the people of all hopes.
At the present time, it is the duty of public men, not to preach blue ruin, but to stand up and set the example to those who are still prepared to hope in better times.
Mr. Speaker, I wish to pay a tribute to the prime minister of this country, for he is a preacher of energy. At no time, since confederation, was there at the head of the Canadian government, a man displaying so much disinterestedness, endowed with such courage and so energetic. No prime minister, no public man, has ever devoted more time, more work to the welfare of his country.
Why, then, try to underestimate his worth or to minimize his merit? I know that some of our opponents would be only too happy should they succeed in reducing to naught the splendid courage and undaunted energy for which the prime minister of Canada is noted.
As long as the people of this country give us their support, we shall give expression to our admiration for his tireless efforts in the service of his country and in the best interests of his fellow citizens.
As to the economic disturbances now existing in nations other than those forming part of the empire, it seems obvious that one of the main obstacles in the way of remedying the depression and forwarding our economical reconstruction, lies in the lack of confidence in the future. Such lack of faith in the future is accountable for by the fear and anxiety prevailing in connection with the political situation in Europe. We had an

United Kingdom
evidence of that fear and of that anxiety in the wranglings that occurred at Geneva between the various members of the League of Nations. These difficulties have been made worse by the uncertainty and distress resulting from the world-wide depression.
The best we Canadians could do in order to improve our economical conditions, would be to foster hope in the future, to trust in the strength of our institutions; to rest our confidence-and that applies to one and all- in those who form part of the League of Nations, and finally, to let no one question the permanence of peace in Europe.
As for us, Canadians, of French extraction, let us be convinced that our present troubles pale into insignifance when compared with what had to be faced by our forebears in the days when the country was in course of settlement and development. The amount of courage and energy displayed by our valiant ancestors were incomparably greater than those required of us to overcome the minor obstacles which confront us nowadays. Were we, to-day, in the same position as these great men were placed in then, how small and different we would be! So I say, when seeking a way out of our difficulties, let us bring to the task some cheerfulness, some courage, some energy, and, I may add, let there be no more talk of defeat or failure; let hope ever be our watchword.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE MOTION FOR APPROVAL OF TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to delay the house for any great length of time because I believe the matter under discussion has been fairly well covered. At all events most of the important points have been covered by previous speakers. It is most gratifying that in an important matter of this kind the speeches have been of a very high order, and there has been a real desire to bring out all the facts concerning the trade agreement.
I wish however to make my position clear. Speaking on the address in reply to the speech from the throne, I stated that when given an opportunity to examine the contents of the agreement I would pass an opinion upon it. I have had the opportunity to make that investigation, and have had the added advantage of listening to the speeches of hon. members in all quarters of the house. I regret to say that I have not changed my opinion, but have been confirmed in the suspicion that under the guise of an imperial preference the agreement simply means additional taxation upon the shoulders of the Canadian people who, at the present time, are ill able to bear it. Without covering the

ground taken by previous speakers I should like to state the position that I, as a member of the Liberal party, have always taken in matters pertaining to trade, and particularly empire trade. Personally, I have always advocated free trade within the British Empire. I am of the opinion that a free exchange of commodities among the constituent parts of that empire would tend to make us more prosperous than we are to-day. I do not wish, however, to have any entanglements which would prevent Canada from trading advantageously with any other country which may wish to trade with her.
That point must be made perfectly clear. Much-nay, the whole-of the distress with which we are faced today can be attributed to the fact that the great trading nations of the world have nationalized themselves, that they have adopted a so-called nationalism, in order that they may live within themselves and restrain trade from crossing their borders. The spectacle we are witnessing today, world-wide in its proportions, is directly attributable to that cause. I am not alone in that opinion, because my view is borne out by almost every economist of note. That was the opinion during the deliberations at Geneva. Therefore one is in good company when making a statement of that kind. I repeat most emphatically that so far as I am concerned I would have no trade barriers whatever between ourselves, the mother country and the sister dominions. At the same time I would not want any entanglements that would prevent Canada from trading, and entering into trade agreements, with any country with which we could do business advantageously.
From 1920-21 to 1930, Mr. Speaker, it was the policy of the Liberal party to reduce tariffs on basic commodities wherever possible, and to seek markets for those commodities wherever we could do business. With regard to the British Empire, and more particularly Great Britain, it was the aim of the previous government to reduce our tariffs to approximately 50 per cent of the duty in effect against foreign countries. That trade prospered; taxation was reduced and unemployment was reduced to a minimum, because no one will deny that we had unemployment in 1922 and 1923. In 1930, however, we had a change of government, with a complete change of policy. As one of the humble members of the Liberal party, and as an elector, I had not the faintest idea that the government now in office would raise the tariff schedules against Great Britain to the extent to which they were raised. I did believe that hon. gentlemen opposite had a mandate from the Can-

adian people to increase tariffs against foreign countries; they made their intention in that regard very clear when they appealed to the public, and the public voted to put them in office. But what did they do? At the special session of 1930, just prior to the imperial conference which was being held for the purpose of extending trade within the empire, they increased the tariff against British goods almost as much as they increased it against products coming from outside countries. They took this action with regard to Great Britain, who had given Canada free entry to her markets for years, and who hoped to be able to continue that policy. Before going to that conference hon. gentlemen opposite took the precaution of putting tariffs almost sky high against British goods coming into Canada, particularly those goods in the manufacture of which the British producer excelled, and which he wished to dispose of in this country.
That was the action they took before the conference was held. When they went to the mother country the proposal of the leader of the Canadian delegation, the Prime Minister, was that although the government had put into effect high tariffs which previously had not applied to British products, British manufacturers would be given a 10 per cent preference in the Canadian market by an increase in the tariff against foreign goods. Can one wonder that the British delegation viewed that proposal with some consternation? Those gentlemen, representing a country who had given Canadian goods free entry to their market for a decade or two, were met with a proposal of that kind. What earthly good was that suggestion to the British manufacturer who could not climb over the high tariff walls put into effect against his product? I must admit that hon. gentlemen opposite were being true to their promise although, as I have said, I was amazed at the extent to which they raised tariffs against Great Britain. As I said before, I believe they were warranted in putting into effect very high tariffs, if you like, against foreign countries; that was one of their pre-election pledges. But if free mtry to the markets of Great Britain was caluable to Canada at that time, has this government done anything to ensure the continuance of that free entry? If Great Britain had acted towards us as we have acted towards that country from 1930 on our attitude would have been one of resentment. I believe I am safe in saying that during the last election the Conservative party profited immensely by the antagonism aroused in the minds of the people by the imposition of almost prohibitive duties against our exports to

the United States, but I do not believe one elector in ten had the faintest idea that our trade with Great Britain, and our free entry into the British market, would be jeopardized by the placing of excessive duties against British goods. Is it any wonder, Mr. Speaker, that the conference resulted as it did? Naturally the British manufacturer wns hoping, that his market in Canada would be increased, so is it any wonder that there was a feeling of resentment, and that the statement by Mr. Thomas was made on that occasion?
In any case nothing was done. Almost two years later we were preparing for another conference, and I did hope that hon. gentlemen opposite-whom I have said had a mandate from the people to impose higher protective duties against foreign goods-were completely satisfied with their work. They must have seen the results of their actions; they must have known that conditions in Canada were immeasurably worse and were not improving at all, and that if anything at all could be done to secure trade it should be done during the progress of the conference. But we found hon. gentlemen opposite with the same attitude with respect to trade within the empire. Surely on textiles, in particular, the British manufacturer could have been given a chance in Canada. Surely some relief could have been given, the overburdened consumer in this country through a reduction in the textile schedules so far as they affect Great Britain. No heed was paid the plea of France for wider markets so far as textiles were concerned, but having in mind all that had taken place in Canada between 1930 and 1932 I did hope that some provision would have been made to widen the market for British products in this country. That was not done; they stuck to their guns. They said that Great Britain, as well as foreign countries, should not ibe allowed to compete with Canadian manufacturers, either those already in existence or those who might come into existence later. That was the attitude in which the Canadian representatives took part in this conference.
When I examine the document now before us I am amazed that so little has been secured that is of real value to the Canadian producer. So far as wheat, copper, zinc, lead, apples and so on are concerned, we have always enjoyed free entry into the British market, so there is nothing new in these provisions. When I come to examine the schedules in regard to other free entries I find that most of those that are at all important concern articles that go into the manufacture of goods in Canadian factories, whose pro-

United Kingdom
ducts are highly protected but who obtain their raw materials free of duty. Is it'any wonder that there is a feeling of resentment at treatment of this character? If our Canadian delegation had been willing to extend our market, do you not think that a better spirit would have prevailed in the conference? Do you not think that a better spirit would be prevailing now? It is very evident, not only in the Canadian government but in the home government as well, that all is not well with respect to this agreement. And -may I point out to you, Mr. Speaker, that this is the first occasion on which an agreement of this kind has been under consideration in either parliament when it was not received with acclaim and passed almost unanimously.
Why do I oppose this agreement? I oppose it because there are 138 articles in it which are of no advantage whatever to the Britisher and which simply fasten on the Canadian consumer a rate of taxation higher than ever before. Do the government expect men who* believe in the fiscal policies in which I believe to support an agreement of this kind? I do not think they do. Perhaps they are right in imposing upon the Canadian people their ideas and policies because they are in power and have the voting strength to do so. But I have my own rights to assert and my own position to protect, and I must do so by protesting against this sort of thing which is bringing so much distress and misery to the people of Canada. I say, there are in this agreement 138 articles in respect of which the government seize the opportunity, under the guise of a British preference, of increasing the duties on goods coming into Canada. Of 100 articles or so which I have examined in the schedules, and which are free or upon which a reduction has taken place, the larger percentage are goods that are used in the manufacture of our raw products in Canada, and the importation is very small. I will mention one, which has been referred to before-cream separators. The occasion is seized to increase the duty by 25 per cent on an article which heretofore has entered free. Why? Because we have Canadian manufacturers making cream separators. Does anyone think that the dairy industry at this moment can stand an added burden of this sort? Yet, under the guise of an imperial preference, the government are asking gentlemen on this side, who have all their lives opposed this sort of thing, to support such an agreement. I cannot believe that the government ever hoped even to have consideration given the agreement by men who, they are aware, throughout their lifetime, have opposed such a policy, and I say further that in my
opinion hon. gentlemen occupying the treasury benches today had no mandate to make an agreement of this kind by which, under the guise of an imperial preference, they increase tariffs to the detriment of the Canadian consumer.
There are a number of items with which I am in entire agreement, and I will say that in so far as these conform to Liberal policies and principles with respect to tariffs, I would support them even if it did not mean business. But, Mr. Speaker, I am precluded from doing so; I dare not do so without being accused of standing for the agreement as a whole. That is my position in this matter. It would be indeed a very poor agreement were there not some provisions in it that were in the interests of the Canadian people-an exceedingly poor agreement. But I confess that they are so few, in an agreement which is so farreaching in its effect upon industry and production, and which is so important to the welfare of the Canadian people, that these changes count for very little. I do not want to cover ground that has already been gone over by hon. gentlemen who have preceded me; suffice it to say that for the reasons I have stated I find myself in a position where I must oppose the treaty.
There is one other matter with regard to which I wish to say a word or two while I am on my feet, although it has very little to do with the treaty itself, except in an indirect way. For my part, I believe that 90 per cent of the difficulties which we are experiencing today can be attributed to the tariff, but there certainly is something to be said with regard to the question of currency. And here again I am astonished to find that in the free entry of goods into Canada currency plays a rather important part. When I come to study the schedules I find that it is still possible in connection with goods entering free into Canada from Great Britain for the government to impose the tax of 3 per cent, which has been instituted since hon. gentlemen came into office. But in addition to that, because, forsooth, the Conservative party are standing for what they are pleased to call sound money, we have a further burden imposed on the importer, which must foe paid by the consumer. I refer to the difference estimated between the Canadian dollar and the pound. Today, I presume, that difference is in the neighbourhood of 68 cents. That will apply to free entries, and against that also I wish to register my strongest protest. I do hope that the Minister of Finance and the Minister of National Revenue will discontinue the application of these vexatious duties to goods imported into this country. They have been

nothing but vexatious impositions since their inception. There is a vast difference between protection, if you are bound to have protection, against slaughter prices in a slaughter market and protection against goods coming into the country simply because those goods happen to come into conflict with goods manufactured in Canada. The government have carried this policy to an extreme which is absolutely unjustifiable, and under this agreement, while there is a veiled promise of reform, while there is a promise that as soon as the financing of Canada will permit, the imposition of these dump duties and other duties of a similar character will be eliminated, nevertheless one is bound to ask in all sincerity whether there is very much prospect of the business of the country improving under the administration at present in office in Canada. Very little demonstration of any improvement has so far been forthcoming, and if I am to judge by past performances I am afraid that there will have to be an entire change of fiscal policy before we can look for very much improvement in the economic situation in Canada. We shall have to relieve my hon. friend the Minister of Finance of the grievous burden he is bearing today. No, Mr. Speaker; the policy is entirely wrong. I have said on many occasions in this house, after having fought for almost forty years against this kind of thing, that I should like to see what the actual results would be if an extreme policy such as we have in force today, were put into operation. Well, I have lived to see it, and I am bound to say-
And glad of it.

No, I am
not glad of it, but I am bound to say that the result has exceeded anything I could conceive in the way of difficulties and tribulation for the people who have enacted it. My only regret is that this has brought so much in the way of sorrow, discomfort, and tribulation to the Canadian people, as well as to the people in every other country in the world. When this government, in the face of unemployment, in the face of distress, in the face of business failures right and left, in the face of the troubles confronting our farmers, had the opportunity to widen the markets for our kith and kin, they refused to do so but, under the guise of imperial agreements, seized the opportunity of fastening more strongly than ever upon the backs and shoulders of the Canadian people the burden of additional protection. I do not think that was the proper spirit in which to approach a conference of this sort.

While this government can attribute its position today to the fact that there was considerable resentment in the public mind against the increases of tariff put into effect by the United States against Canada, how do they think our overseas cousins feel about the attitude they have taken toward them? Can they be happy under it. I should say not. Is it any wonder that when Great Britain did decide to put into effect a moderate tariff they left the doors wide open in order to see what the Canadian government would do about it. Since I have become aware of the provisions of this agreement, I have marvelled at the fact that the British government did not put into effect against Canada the tariff schedules which now apply against other countries. When we realize how we have treated them with respect to imports into this country, the action they have taken speaks well for their generosity. I can only attribute the action they have taken, generous as it is, to the fact that they hope that within a short time better judgment will prevail in this country and we will again return to the old, happy relationships which existed prior to 1930. The sooner we return to those days, the better. We have at least let the people of England know that this attitude is not the attitude of all the people of Canada. This government is in office with a majority of over 200,000 votes, but there are many pepple who, had they known, that these duties were to be put into effect against the mother country, would not have marked their ballots for the Conservative candidates. When they have become fully aware of what they have done, then I am certain that there will be no doubt about what they will do.
It was my hope that we might have had a very full discussion upon the schedules, and with that in mind I spent considerable time in studying them. I may say that I can heartily support some of them which are along the lines I have advocated continuously, but my regret is that there are not more. I cannot see why this government could not have widened the avenues of trade within the empire and have made conditions easier for the Canadian people. However, they have decided not to do so, but rather to increase the intermediate and general tariffs which make the situation more difficult. As far as the schedules are concerned, no opportunity is given to me to express an opinion thereon. I must first vote upon the motion now before the house and because of t}ie principles which I have always advocated and which I firmly believe to be in the best interests of the Canadian people, that vote must be against the agreement.

That the resolution be amended by adding the following:
That this motion be not put until after the fiscal changes proposed by the rates set forth in schedule E attached to said agreement and forming a part thereof, which schedule of rates has been referred by this house to its committee of ways and means, have been considered in said committee.

I am afraid the amendment which the hon. member seeks to move is not in order.
Why?

For these reasons: the
resolution which the house is now discussing approves only of the trade agreement therein referred to "subject to the legislation required in order to give effect to the fiscal changes consequent thereto," using the actual words of the motion. An unqualified approval is not sought. The legislation referred to in the resolution includes schedule E referred to in the amendment. This is not a motion which can be amended by stating any special reason for not agreeing to the principle of the question of being opposed to its progress. To move that it be not put is not an amendment. If it is desired that the question be not now put, it is open to any hon. member to move the previous question and to vote it down under standing order 55. Although the mover and seconder of the previous question generally vote in its favour, there is no rule to prevent their voting against their own motion. I quote Bourinot, fourth edition, at page 327 as follows:
The members proposing and seconding the previous question generally vote in its favour but there is no rule to prevent them voting against their own motion.
I therefore declare the amendment as presented as not in order.

Mr. Speaker,
before your ruling is finally given, I should like to say that I do not interpret the amendment as saying that the motion shall not be put; it rather seeks to fix a time at which it shall be put, a time which will permit a full discussion in the interval of the tariff changes contained in the agreement. The agreement is meaningless without the schedule, which forms a part thereof, in fact the several tariff items contained in the schedule are the most important part of the agreement. The amendment does not say that Your Honour shall not put the motion which is to approve the agreement, it says that that motion shall not be put until the house has had an opportunity of discussing the tariff items in the agreement, which items are now before the committee of ways and means for consideration. All that is necessary to serve the ends of the amendment is that this debate be discontinued until an opportunity has been afforded of discussing tariff items in committee of ways and means. Surely we should not be asked to give our approval to an agreement without knowing what the effect of the schedule, which is its main feature, is going to be.
Your Honour will have observed, from what has already been said, that this agreement in its effect is not so much an agreement to increase trade between Canada and Great Britain as it is an agreement to make increasingly difficult trade between the British Empire, particularly Canada, and other countries of the world. That at least is our contention, and we believe that this will be established the moment this agreement is considered in relation to the tariff items which appear in the schedule. If it can he shown we are wrong in this, we are, I hope, open-minded enough to be prepared to reconsider the opposition we have to the agreement itself. Our position is that this agreement primarily is one to increase tariffs rather than to decrease tariffs. That point can be definitely determined only by discussion of the tariff items in committee. Till it is determined we should not be asked to approve the agreement.

MURPHY (Minister of the Interior) : Mr. Speaker, I do rise not with the expectation that I can add very materially to this rather detailed debate, but rather because I desire to place myself on record unreservedly as being in favour of this resolution and the agreement on which it is based. Members of every shade of political faith in the house have expressed their individual opinions, as well as the general opinion of the party to 
which they give allegiance, concerning the merits or demerits of the resolution now before the house.
It might be well, Mr. Speaker, in order to obtain a proper perspective, to consider why we, in this year 1932, are debating such a resolution; why the economic conferences of 1930 and 1932 were held; why the representatives of the component parts of the British Empire or the British commonwealth of nations assented wholeheartedly, hopefully and unreservedly to the various agreements that were signed in this chamber, and one of which we are now debating. To answer that question one would have to go very far back into history to find the first cause, but the more immediate causes date from the outbreak of the world war in 1914.
During those four years of carnage there was a tremendous loss. There was a loss of millions of workers, a shortage of food and raw materials, a dislocation of trade and industry, yes, Mr. Speaker, and in their wake there followed starvation and impoverishment. We have a very lively recollection of those four years. We know of the starvation and impoverishment that then existed and when that war was over, the first task of suffering humanity was to build a framework within which man could once again carry on his usual avocations; in other words, to make, to sell and to consume, to clear the old channels of trade and to make new ones, and in addition to that to restore a single and stable medium of exchange. To the great surprise- and I think I am correct in saying this-of all people, there was an apparent success, a success that exceeded the hopes of even the most optimistic. By the year 1925 world production had increased 18 per cent and the population had increased six per cent. Currencies were again linked with gold and we had a single and stable medium of exchange.
During the next four years progress was indeed more rapid than it had been during the previous seven years. Trade was flowing more freely and the common peoples, so termed, of the world had a higher standard of living and better labour conditions than ever before. But may I say here that linked with that recovery was an intense economic nationalism which was adopted by practically all countries which had engaged in the conflict. That was due' to one thing and one thing only, and that was fear. During those years of war the people had no sense of security and when the war was over, that is what they wanted more than anything else. They desired to attain that security and the means adopted to attain it were in most cases tariffs. They

United Kingdom
endeavoured to make themselvea self-supporting as far as possible. It had been impressed upon them during the war years that they were dependent upon other parts of the world for their very life, for their foodstuffs. That was the situation.
As I said a moment ago, there was a remarkable recovery. But following that we had a collapse, a rout, a debacle greater in intensity and range than in all previous experiences. Canada was caught in that maelstrom of events and she was possibly harder hit because she is a primary producer. Canada produces and sells mostly her primary products and we are all aware that the prices of primary products are the first to fall and the last to rise. That applies particularly to the products of the field, the forest, the mine and the sea.
Farming is still our principal industry in Canada. In fact, in 1931, 32-8 per cent of
those gainfully employed were engaged in farming, and 38-2 per cent of the total so gainfully employed were males. We have in Canada a large agricultural population and we export immense quantities of agricultural products, the principal one of which is wheat. So much is that the case that wheat with flour accounted for over 36 per cent of the total exports of our produce in 1929. This proves conclusively that the economic structure of Canada is -built up, to a great extent, in relation to the production and export of wheat. I would say that our policy is this: (a) Taking all factors into consideration, to protect our producers against unfair competition in the home market; (fo) to trade and exchange goods with all other countries which are prepared to deal with us on a fair basis and to find new markets. Our goods have been shut out of other countries by hostile tariffs, restricting our markets, over the years, and we are endeavouring at the present time to enlarge our markets, and one method among others that we have adopted is shown in the agreements before us.
The situation that confronted Canada and all other empire countries before the economic conference took place was, as everyone knows, one of appalling collapse in world trade. We are told in the World Economic Survey, issued as recently as August of this year by the League of Nations, that the total value of world trade fell from roundly $59,000,000,000 in 1929 to $34,000,000,000 in 1931. Although it sounds incredible, that brief period witnessed the disappearance of $25,000,000,000 worth of trade, part of that huge amount vanishing simply through the fall of prices, and the balance through actual stoppage in the flow of commodities.
That strangulation of trade has laid its hand upon Canada as upon all other countries but to say that Canadian policy has been a contributory factor is to misread the whole sequence of world conditions and events. Canada's loss of commerce has been heavy because we have, as a country, been heavily engaged in external trade for many years j but the very magnitude of the world trade decline should be enough to convince everyone that any attempt to lay at Canada's door any share of responsibility for the commercial calamity from which we are suffering is to magnify beyond all reason Canada's actual power to influence world affairs.

Mr. Speaker, the debate on this conference agreement has taken up much of the time of the house; I had not intended to take part in it until the developments of the last day or two made me feel I should say something in regard to this agreement. I shall try not to be very long, as I think the house should endeavour to get this question settled and proceed to a discussion of other vital matters which, in my opinion, should be decided before parliament adjourns for the Christmas recess. The government should have allowed the house to discuss these proposals in committee first. The house has already been moved into committee of ways and means for the purpose and had we been allowed to discuss the schedules in committtee first, I do not think this long debate upon the agreement itself would have been necessary. But the discussion has been well worth while, some points have come to light that I think were not evident on a cursory perusal of the proposal as brought down.
After listening to the debate for the last two weeks I would endeavour to sum up at least part of the results of this conference by saying that although much was expected, not only by the government but by the country, the results achieved have not been up to the expectations of the public. The conference was heralded by many as being a means of ending the depression, but in reality it has failed to deal with the root causes of the depression, namely the lack of purchasing power among the different peoples of the empire and of the world. It was anticipated that as a result of this conference international trade would be increased. I do not think there is going to be any increase in trade at all. Apparently there is only to be a diversion of trade between Canada and other countries outside the empire to new channels of trade between Canada, the United Kingdom, and the other countries of the empire.

The point of order having been settled, I shall proceed to say what I intended to say in the first place. I was saying that at the imperial conference of 1930 the Prime Minister made his offer of a two-way preference to the British government, and in this he was supported by the other dominions. The MacDonald government in power at that time declined to accept his proposal. Our Prime Minister, however, amplified his proposal, asked the mother country to think it over and invited the British dominions to a conference at Ottawa. The people of Great Britain considered the matter very seriously, and, when the opportunity presented itself, voted the present British government into office with an overwhelming mandate to establish protection and to enter into reciprocal relations with the outlying parts of the empire. The Prime Minister of Canada seized the opportunity and renewed his proposal for a conference in Ottawa. AH parts of the empire accepted the proposal, and the result was the most impreissive gathering in the history of the British commonwealth of nations.
I might point out here that the Prime Minister of Canada seems to have a special faculty for seizing the proper moment to do anything. This is not the first occasion on which he has seized the proper moment to put into effect the policies for which he stands. May I direct your attention, sir, to the fact that he did so on another very important occasion when in 1930 he submitted to this country his proposal for the liquidation of our outstanding debt. Had he waited longer, it is doubtful whether since then the revision of those debts could have been accomplished.
Each delegation at the conference considered the welfare of its own territory, but overshadowing all selfish considerations was the ultimate welfare of the empire as a whole. The result is a series of twelve trade agreements based upon the Bennett policy.
Great Britain now imposes tariffs on many foreign primary products, while similar empire products are admitted free of duty. Many Canadian manufactured products now have free entry to the British market, while their foreign competitors must pay duty. As an equalizing factor the preferences previously extended to British manufacturers have been increased by either greater British preferences or higher tariffs to foreign nations. This has opened up for Canadian manufacturers fair competition in the British market, while we extend to Britain the same opportunity in our market. Thus is the manufacturer given reasonable opportunity, while at the same time

the government has taken care that the consumer is not exploited.
Under the agreements which we are considering Canada obtains wider openings in the United Kingdom and other empire countries for her farm products, base metals, other primary products and a long list of manufactured articles. The economists of the world agree that there are three causes for the present depression, although they are not at one as to their respective importance: first, war debts; second tariffs, and third, the collapse of our monetary system. We could hardly expect such a conference to do very much with regard to war debts. War debts involve both external and internal debts; they involve the interest on bonds, and have to do with such things as taxes and wages. One economist says that if the prices of manufactured products, the interest on our debts, the interest on our bonds and on our mortgages, and our taxes had all fallen in the same proportion as have the prices we receive for our farm commodities, then we would have no cause to complain ; but these various charges, fixed and unalterable, act as a drag on the wheel and prevent a return to prosperity. That is what one man calls rigidity. Nothing whatever was done at the conference in that regard. In fact the government has increased this rigidity, because when it put through a loan not long ago it ran up the rate of interest to 5.17 per cent instead of bringing it down as the British government did, and thus adding to the burden which the people are carrying.

One of the unfortunate legacies of the conference is the bitterness and ill-will created between the British and Canadian delegates.
We all know, it was common knowledge on the streets in Ottawa, that this was just a cat-and-dog fight. There were hard things said. How can it help to join Canada closer to the empire and Great Britain closer to Canada when we find articles such as this in the News-Chronicle of September 16, 1932:
They will never let it be known, for instance, what actually took place behind the scenes of an imperial gathering which at times degenerated into a ferocious dog fight.
No British minister will ever say in public what has undoubtedly been said in private about the behaviour and bearing of Mr. Bennett, president of the conference, Prime Minister of Canada, and the world's prize bully.
These hard things have been said, and they leave an impression. It is unfortunate that they should be said. The article goes on:
No minister, compelled for political reasons to make the best of a bad job and to perpetuate an illusion will ever say in public what I am pretty sure has been said often enough in private in heart to heart talks among members of the British government, that one more conference like that so dismally concluded at Ottawa will be sufficient to smash the empire to pieces.
As long as I live I shall not forget that appalling scene at the final plenary session in the parliament house when disgust and loathing were revealed as plainly on the faces of exhausted delegates as if they had been impressed there with a rubber stamp.
I went to Ottawa fearing the worst but hoping for the best. I came away more con-

United Kingdom
vinced than I have been about anything in politics that the most ineffably perfect method of dissolving a great modern empire is to embark with a flourish of trumpets on an imperial tariff bargaining battle.
The seven British ministers were honourable and reasonably competent men, anxious to safeguard the interests of their country, and willing at the same time to do what they could for the empire and for world trade. Within seven days their noble sentiments were swamped in the bog of national and sectional self-interest. Within forty-eight hours all the representatives of the selfish industrial interests of the empire emerged into the light like repulsive insects from beneath a raised stone in the' mud. In less than a week all the beautiful imperial talk of imperial unity and imperial sacrifice had been washed off the imperial slate with a dirty sponge.
One of the strangest of the many strange underground spectacles at Ottawa was that of Lord Hailsham and Mr. Neville Chamberlain compelled as responsible statesmen to talk sound free trade doctrine in defence of British trade. It was a spectacle which infuriated dominion politicians and drove Mr. Bennett himself into recurring fits of hysteria.
Sayings like that, Mr. Speaker, do not foster good-will or peace or harmony. These are some of the results of the conference in relation to the empire. I believe that instead of drawing the empire closer together it has made the ties of empire more fragile and therefore more likely to be broken.
I come to the Canadian viewpoint, and I wish to deal with that more particularly. Let me refer first to some of the things that we get. As I look over the list, the thing that has been talked about more than any other is the preference on wheat; but when I read article 4, all the benefits in regard to wheat disappear. The hon. member for Qu'Appelle, speaking of this, said that when in 1896 the Liberal government came into power they took the tariff off barbed wire and immediately the price went up. Conversely, Mr. Speaker, if you put a tariff on, the price will go down. Probably that is why the price of wheat has fallen-they put on a preference of six cents and immediately the price went down. And our farmers in western Canada said: "Thank heaven it wasn't twelve cents." It had fallen six cents, and the moment the tariff schedules were put out it fell another six cents. So I suppose if we had got a preference of twelve cents it would have fallen twelve cents immediately, and later on would have fallen another twelve.
The Minister of the Interior (Mr. Murphy), speaking this afternoon-or rather in reading his speech-quoted a lot of figures in regard to wheat. I asked him what those figures were based on, whether on the Fort William price, the country elevator price, seaboard
prices, or what, and he did not tell me. Whether or not he was unable to tell me I do not know; probably the man who wrote the speech did not mention the place. At any rate he was not able to inform me on that point. Figures about the amount of wheat we export are all very well, but the thing of chief importance to the farmers is the price. With world conditions such as they are now, the farmers cannot live on the farm and pay their taxes. In western Canada farm after farm is being forsaken and people are leaving, unable to make a living on the land.
We find that the agreement is a sort of half-baked agreement; it is like a lot of other legislation we have had brought before us- ill-conceived, half-baked, half-digested, and when it comes here we are able to point to all sorts of flaws in it. For example, we do not know at present whether or not Canadian wheat stored in Buffalo can be shipped to England and be entitled to the preference. The amount of wheat going to Great Britain via the United States is very great, in fact a large percentage of the Canadian wheat used in England goes via the United States. The United States will have a boat load of wheat to be sold. They will inquire as to the world price. They will offer it to Germany or to Italy and will take one, two, three, four or five cents less from those countries, and still receive as high a price as they would in England. That will be the tendency-to lower the price on the markets of the world, and incidentally lower the price we will receive in England. Let hon. members make no mistake about that. The marketing of wheat from the Argentine, from the United States and other countries will have a tendency to lower our wheat price. We believe that will be detrimental rather than beneficial.
Either the hon. member for Camrose (Mr. Lucas) or the hon. member for Kindersley (Mr. Carmichael), speaking on this agreement, stated that he thought this preference might be some good and for that reason he was going to vote for it; that if the agreement was approved a six cent preference would be afforded. Why, this government will be defeated; we will go to the country and a Liberal government will be returned to provide preferences which will be of some use to us.
Oh, oh.

It is all right for hon. members to say "oh, oh", but let me tell my hon. friends opposite that if they went to the country today very few Tories would come back; make no mistake about that-only one of my hon. friends opposite would come back from the prairies. I know the spirit and the feeling of the farmers in the west. They know they have been fooled long enough. Promises have been made to them which were not kept; yes, they were fooled with promises wliich were not fulfilled. They were told they would receive higher prices for their wheat, their butter, their eggs-yes, for everything they sold. Every plateform on which hon. members stood was dangerous. They were just-promises; we remember all about it, although hon. members opposite like to forget them.
The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Weir) tells me that about 200,000 pounds of Canadian butter was shipped back from England; it could not be sold there. Some of it was sent back to this country; it could not be readmitted unless duty was paid, so it was 
shipped back to England-I suppose that was done in order to ripen it on the ocean-and another attempt was made to sell it upon its return to England. And butter is coming in from New Zealand; perhaps some of our friends opposite are eating the New Zealand butter they disliked so much.
The hon. member for Qu'Appelle stated he could sell his grain for 60 cents a bushel if he could receive five cents per pound for his hogs and cattle on the hoof. I say if it were not. for that word "if" you might be able to do it; but you cannot get that much, that is all there is to it. I wonder if the hon. member ever heard the story about the dog and the rabbit. Well, the dog didn't run fast enough. That is the trouble with the prices the hon. member mentioned; he is not able to get that price for his cattle.

hon. members have said that already industry is deriving benefit from the trade pact. Yes, we are beginning to feel it all right; it is beginning to pinch a little tighter all the time. In South Huron the Minister of Agriculture said he had saved the farmers of Canada over $36,000,000. I looked all over the country and could find no farmers who had received any of that money. Certainly the farmers in the west got none of it. I have asked the ex-Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) if any benefit was received in the province of Quebec, and he said there was not. The question was asked of the farmers during the campaign in South Huron-and they only laughed at it; they thought it was a big joke. Whether any of that money was in their pockets, but they replied that their pockets were empty. My hon. friend opposite seems to be one of those bloated aristocrats; he looks well kept-perhaps he is getting some of it. Anyway there is no doubt that the farmers did not get it. Anyway there is no doubt that the farmers did not get it.
But I must hurry on and refer to one or two further points. Let me draw attention of hon. members to crude oil. For some reason one of the regulations in the customs tariff concerning crude oil has been eliminated. I do not know whether Russian oil was the cause of it. I wish to thank the Prime Minister for admitting that the committee which dealt with gasoline prices was right, anyway. Last year when we made representations before the committee on banking and commerce dealing with gasoline

it seemed we were all wrong; practically all members opposite voted against us. While in my constituency the hon. member for Regina (Mr. Turnbull), whether from ignorance or from some other cause, stated that the Liberal government had placed tariffs on gasoline just as high as those imposed by the Conservative government. I might be able to excuse a layman who did not know better, but for a member of parliament and a lawyer to stand on a public platform and make a statement of that kind is as bad as the statements made concerning the price of butter. Those statements were made either through ignorance or in an attempt to deceive the public-one or the other. I wish to thank the Prime Minister for taking the dumping duty off gasoline, and showing that we were right when we contended that we were paying too much for that commodity.
I believe if he looked into the matter more closely he would find good reason for a further reduction in the duty on gasoline; he would be taking a step in the right direction.

And we need coal.

our country we need it, because it is cold up there.
One other point and then I have finished. The hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. Fraser), the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Weir), and the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Willis), referred to the valley of humiliation.
An hen. MEMBER: Hear, hear.

Oh yes, "hear, hear." I tell my hon. friend if I were one of the mercenaries in the Conservative army who had been bought and paid for I would not say that. Go and ask the member for Regina, who says you were bought and paid for. Seven hundred and fifty thousand dollars was your price.
Let me read what the Vancouver Sun has to say. The hon. member for Cariboo read some advertisements from that paper; I shall read an editorial. It says:
Prominently displayed in the Tory press throughout Canada is the statement of F. W. Turnbull, K.C., member of parliament for Regina, who boldly admits that R. B. Bennett contributed $750,000 of his own money to the Conservative campaign funds.
And Mr. Turnbull naively adds, "Not much more than that was spent."
Heaven only knows how much more than $750,000 Mr. Bennett threw into the pot. But the self-conscious manner in which the Tory press parades this admission is proof in itself of the deep resentment every Conservative must feel over the purchase of the party by rich and opulent R. B. Bennett. For that is just what it amounts to.
Mr. Bennett, to make himself Prime Minister, bought the party and paid for it. And he is conscious of his ownership. That is why he feels so free to order his cabinet around like a flock of school boys, to thump the table and dictate to everybody.
Perhaps that is why, too, he felt so free to piously dedicate his life five times over to the service of the party. Mr. Bennett certainly violated no item in his creed of selfishness when he dedicated himself to himself.
Mr. Bennett, then, bought his premiership for three-quarters of a million dollars. Where did he get the money? How much of it came from Canadian Pacific Railway real estate operations in Calgary? How much of it was derived from his Imperial Oil associations? How much of it came out of the pockets of the late Mrs. Eddy? Surely the public is entitled to know the origin of all campaign funds.
Under our system there is nothing legally wrong with a man making money as Mr. Bennett made it. But if a man, by such methods, gets together six or eight million dollars and then goes out and buys the government of his country, he is doing the very thing, in principle, for which corporations are unhesitatingly condemned.
What is the difference between a corporation giving $750,000 to a political party in order to secure material favours for itself and Mr. Bennett paying $750,000 for the privilege of owning and bossing not only Conservatives but the whole nation? Such things thwart the very spirit of democratic government.
Mr. Bennett has personally bought the Conservative party; he owns it.
His strutting attitude of proprietorship and his air of owning the country remind Conservatives that they are chattels rather than colleagues, and remind Canadians that they are serfs rather than citizens.
This has been referred to not only in the Conservative press; we find the Conservative

May I say, Mr. Speaker, that there is reason to believe that the passing of this agreement will affect what may take place at the world economic conference, and that you cannot separate the two in the bearing of the one upon the other. I wish to give your honour my reasons for so believing. In an Associated Press despatch from London dated October 22 I find the following:
Sir Walter Layton, noted economist, announced his resignation Tuesday from the preparatory committee of the world economic conference because of a "serious difference of opinion" between himself and the British government.
He said he had differed with Neville Chamberlain, chancellor of the exchequer, on "What further action is required in order to restore reasonable freedom to the movement of international trade?"

In a letter to Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald, Sir Walter wrote, "The government view is that the desired result can be obtained through individual negotiations with foreign countries within limits set by the Ottawa agreements and subject to strict insistence on our 'most favoured nation' rights."
"Judging from past experience, however," the letter to the premier continued, "I fear the method of bilateral negotiation will make very little impression on the protectionist system of the world as a whole, as it has grown up since the war. In my opinion, the financial situation in which Great Britain finds herself at this moment, taken in conjunction with the immense importance of the British market to the whole world, gives us the unique opportunity-in collaboration with countries already on a low tariff basis and those to whom restoration of foreign trade is a vital necessity
to propound and press forward plans conceived on much bolder and broader lines."
Sir Walter pointed out permanent tariffs and meat quotas, as barriers to world agreements, and declared stabilization of the British pound "depends essentially on whether we secure reasonable level tariffs or contemplate international trade will continue to be cribbed and confined."
There can be no doubt at all that this very agreement which we are considering here is being interpreted by the government in Great Britain as placing restrictions upon the discussions that may occur, and the possible course of action that may be taken, at the world economic conference. Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett), made his appearance in the house, the other day, to disclose the tariff changes resulting from the Imperial conference agreements, he had the inspired bearing of Moses carrying the Tables of the Law!
