We now see more dearly, especially after the enlightening speech of the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) and the systematic and logical arguments of those who took part in this debate, on this side of the house. For you will admit, sir, that the discusssion was all one sided. Here and there voices rose on the opposite side, but it was simply to sing vague refrains on old tunes. The house did not much appreciate this music in minor mode. It also noted that the main theme was forgotten. For it was a matter of knowing, exactly, what these agreements we are asked to approve comprised and what chances they offered to increase our trade and to lighten the burden of the crisis which has reached all classes of our population.
Reference to these were hardly made in the few speeches of our friends opposite, unless it was, as their leader did, to beg the Canadians to repose their trust in the new promises a hundred times renewed.
Thus at the beginning of the week we heard the hon. member for Montmagny (Mr. LaVergne) state that if he were Liberal, he would advise the Liberal party to approve the agreements before the house without even discussing them. The hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency (Mr. Dorion) delivered, today, a somewhat dispassionate speech, but he could not end his speech without disparaging again Quebec, without stating to the members of the various provinces that Quebec was badly administered. He even criticized the provincial department of agriculture, because this department was not doing anything to relieve the farmers. Was it bad faith on his part or was it through ignorance? Truly, I think, it was both. Yet the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency is not without knowing that it is the province of Quebec which expends the most to foster agriculture, considering the taxes levied on the people. It ill suited a Conservative member to criticize the Quebec government, when hon. gentlemen opposite, last year, decreased the farm appropriations by $3,000,000; at a time when they were advocating the policy of back to the land. The hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency has a hobby of attacking distinguished men, as he did today. He attacked Taschereau, Lapointe and Mackenzie King. This, sir, reminds me of a peculiarity which we note in our rural districts and which must equally occur in the Yukon. Since the automobile has made its appearance, we find what one may call a breed of family dogs, somewhat old and fat, they seem to be of little use, but the farmers, however, keep them because they were of some service to the family in the past. They are not wicked nor do they bite neighbours, they are even in the habit of licking the hands of passing beggars because dogs have an instinct that they are dependent as these beggars are. However, when an automobile or a vehicle appears which they are unable to follow, immediately they start barking behind the fMr. Fafard.]
vehicle until it disappears in the distance. This somewhat applies to the member for Quebec-Montmorency-whom I do not look upon as a dog for such is not the case-he always attacks someone big because he cannot follow his vehicle or political career.
After being in power two years, this government has found nothing better to do than to make new pledges. The only difference is that instead of making oral promisee, as those we have so often heard, they are now written down in a treaty. This is no guarantee, as we shall see. First they are indefinite. They depend on circumstances like those made by Mr. Bennett, previous to the election. We now are aware that Tory pledges are unreliable, when conditions are not favourable. There was nothing under the skies that the leader of the Conservative party did not promise, relying on an improvement in the situation. Unemployment, for instance was inevitably to disappear with the improvement, in the near future, of business. Banking on this, the Conservative leader pledged himself to make it disappear. He relied especially on his lucky star! When the Conservative party assumed power the unemployed numbered 250,000. Since then their number has doubled and even trebled, according to the statistics recently given out by the government. The Imperial economic conference was to solve this problem which overshadows all the others in importance and which should be our first care.
Hon. gentlemen opposite laughed when my hon. friend the member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe) stated that he had prayed for the success of the Imperial conference. It is only necessary to have been a witness to the distress prevailing in our cities and rural districts, it is only sufficient to have noted the fortitude and patience of our people in the face of adversity, so as to be moved with the deepest feeling of sympathy. And this sympathy to be real should be expressed in prayers.
